He clerked for Judge Andrew Oldham of the U.S. Fifth Circuit and Judge Danny Boggs of the U.S. Sixth Circuit, and he was an attorney at Butler Snow LLP in Austin before his appointment. record.text: Appointed by Gov. Greg Abbott in March 2025 to the 250th District Court in Travis County, for a term running through December 31, 2026.

candidates.background: Kevin Jewell is a Houston appellate judge seeking the chief justice seat being vacated by Chief Justice Tracy Christopher. candidates.background: Bert Richardson has served on the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals since 2015 and is leaving that statewide seat to run for chief justice of the San Antonio-based Fourth Court of Appeals. He was an assistant district attorney in Bexar County and an assistant U.S. attorney for the Western District of Texas, was appointed to the 379th District Court by Gov. George W. Bush in 1999, and later served as a senior visiting judge. He holds an undergraduate degree from Brigham Young University and a law degree from St. Mary's University School of Law, and is board certified in criminal law.

priorities.text: Says he will treat all cases before the Fourth Court of Appeals with equal right.
Describes his approach as faithfully following the laws of Texas and says his opinions reflect a conservative-minded approach to the law.
Campaigns on 37 years as a trial and appellate lawyer and judge as preparation to lead the court as chief justice.

record.text: Elected to the Court of Criminal Appeals in 2014 and re-elected in 2020.

Joined the 2021 Court of Criminal Appeals majority holding that Attorney General Ken Paxton lacked authority to unilaterally prosecute election fraud cases; he told the San Antonio Report he stands by the ruling.
Served on the 379th District Court from 1999 until losing the 2008 election to Ron Rangel, then served as a senior visiting judge from 2009 to 2014.

candidates.current_role: Judge, 57th District Court (Bexar County), since 2009
candidates.background: Antonia "Toni" Arteaga is a West Texas native and the first woman elected to Bexar County's 57th Civil District Court, where she has served since winning election in 2008. Before that she practiced criminal and civil law with a focus on family law, tried more than 70 jury trials, and was twice appointed a criminal magistrate judge. She holds a B.A. in government and sociology from the University of Texas at Austin and a J.D. from St. Mary's University School of Law (2000). She won the 2026 Democratic primary over Fourth Court Justice Velia Meza.

priorities.text: Says the chief justice of a 32-county appellate court needs executive experience and that her long trial court career prepares her for it.
Says she would aim to issue clear, timely opinions that give trial judges and the public legal certainty.
Describes the appellate court's role as ensuring decisions are grounded in the record and free from abuse of discretion.

promises.text: Says she would aim to provide clear and timely opinions as an appellate justice.

record.text: Has presided over the 57th District Court since 2009, handling complex civil litigation, and is in her fifth term.
Twice served as president of the Texas Association of District Judges, which represents district courts' needs before the Legislature.

notes.text: State Bar of Texas 2026 Judicial Poll (all primary candidates): Bert Richardson 176 votes, Arteaga 109, Velia J. Meza 65. The State Bar poll was a non-scientific survey of participating lawyers taken before the March 2026 primaries.
Founding member of Texas Latinx Judges and Bexar County chair of the National Association of Women Judges, according to texasjudges.org.
Texasjudges.org lists endorsements from the North East Bexar County Democrats and the Bexar County Young Democrats.
If she wins, Gov. Greg Abbott would appoint a replacement to her district court seat, according to the San Antonio Report.

issue_notes.summary: Says the chief justice role requires executive and legislative experience, citing her leadership of the Texas Association of District Judges.

candidates.background: Brian Walker is a native Texan and a justice on the Fort Worth-based Second Court of Appeals.
